The status split is handled by mapping both new fields onto our existing single state, keeping our domain model unchanged for now; a follow-up may expose the extra detail, but nothing needs it today. Unit conversion moves to the boundary, so metres enter the system in metres and the three places that currently convert are deleted.

The recorded fixtures are regenerated from the vendor's published samples rather than from live calls, so the suite stays offline. A feature flag selects the version for one release so a rollback does not require a deploy, and the flag is removed in the following release. The vendor's deprecation date is noted in the client's header comment with the flag's removal tied to it.

title: Split the notification module into transport and policy
question: Should the notification module be split into transport and policy as described?
markdown:
## Summary

The notification module is a single file of about twelve hundred lines mixing three concerns: deciding whether to notify, rendering the message, and delivering it. Every change to a delivery detail risks the policy, and the tests mock the transport to test the policy, which makes them slow and brittle.

## Change

Split the module into three: a policy unit that decides and returns an intent, a renderer that turns an intent into a message, and a transport that delivers. The policy becomes a pure function of its inputs and is tested without any mock; the renderer is tested against fixtures; the transport keeps the existing integration test.

No behaviour changes. The split is mechanical, verified by running the existing suite before and after against the same fixtures, and the public entry point keeps its signature so callers are untouched. Two helpers that were duplicated between the delivery paths collapse into one. The file that remains at the old path re-exports nothing: callers already import the entry point, and the three that imported internals are corrected in this change.

title: Make the report generation timeout configurable
question: Should the report generation timeout be raised and made configurable?
markdown:
## Summary

Report generation has a hard-coded timeout of thirty seconds. The largest tenant's quarterly report now takes between thirty-five and fifty seconds to build, so it fails every time, and the only way to produce it has been to run the generator by hand with the timeout edited out.

## Change

Raise the default to one hundred and twenty seconds and read it from configuration, so a deployment can tune it without a release. The value is validated at start-up to be between ten and six hundred seconds, and a value outside that range fails the process rather than being silently clamped.

The generator also gains progress reporting: every five seconds it records rows processed, so a slow report can be distinguished from a stuck one, which is not currently possible. The request handler returns immediately with a job identifier for reports estimated above fifteen seconds, and the client polls, which removes the dependence on any timeout for the largest cases. The runbook entry describing the manual workaround is deleted, since following it after this change would be wrong.

title: Stabilise the flaky scheduler test
question: Should the scheduler test be stabilised by injecting a controlled clock?
markdown:
## Summary

The scheduler test fails on roughly one run in twelve. It schedules a task fifty milliseconds ahead, sleeps sixty, and asserts the task ran. On a loaded runner the sleep is not enough, and the failure is reported as a scheduler bug, which it is not.

## Change

Inject a clock into the scheduler and give the test a manual implementation it advances explicitly. The test then schedules, advances past the due time, drains the queue and asserts, with no sleeping and no dependence on runner load. Three other tests in the same file follow the same pattern and are converted in the same change.

The production path takes the system clock through the same interface, so there is one code path rather than a test-only branch. The suite loses about four seconds. A lint rule forbidding sleeps in this test directory is added, with the two remaining legitimate uses marked explicitly, so the pattern does not come back. The scheduler's own interface is unchanged and no caller is affected.

title: Put the new ranking behind a flag and measure it
question: Should the new ranking be put behind a feature flag and measured as described?
markdown:
## Summary

The replacement ranking function is ready and scores better on the offline set, but the offline set is drawn from last year's traffic and over-represents one query shape. Shipping it outright would make a regression hard to attribute.

## Change

Put the new ranking behind a flag, default off, evaluated per request from a stable hash of the session so a user's results do not flip between pages. Roll out at one per cent, then ten, then fifty, with a day at each step.

Both rankings emit the same metrics, labelled by variant: result click-through at the first position, time to first click, and the rate of searches refined without a click, which is our clearest signal of a bad result set. A guard switches the flag off automatically if the refinement rate for the new variant exceeds the old by more than two points over an hour, so a bad step does not need a person awake. The flag and the old ranking are removed in a follow-up once the fifty per cent step has held for a week.
